bank.q: The NHS should stay publicly funded and free at the point of use; private involvement should be rolled back.
bank.ctx: The NHS, founded in 1948, provides healthcare free at the point of use, funded by taxes — a source of national pride. This wants it kept public, with private involvement rolled back. It faces record waiting lists and funding strain. The stake is preserving a fully public health service.

bank.q: The NHS is a bloated monopoly; more private provision and competition would cut the waiting lists that are killing people.
bank.ctx: This argues the NHS has become an inefficient state monopoly whose waiting lists cost lives, and that more private provision and competition would speed up care, as in many European mixed systems. The stake is whether markets could fix the NHS or would undermine it.

bank.q: Immigration to Britain is far too high and is changing the country beyond recognition.
bank.ctx: This argues immigration to Britain — which hit record net levels after Brexit — is far too high and is changing the country too fast. It is a defining issue for the right and drove support for Reform UK. The stake is how much immigration Britain can absorb.

bank.q: Immigrants keep the NHS, care homes, and economy running; Britain needs them, not fewer of them.
bank.ctx: This is the pro-immigration view: that migrants staff the NHS, care homes, farms, and hospitality, and that an ageing Britain depends on them. Supporters note the health service would collapse without foreign-born workers. The stake is immigration's role in keeping Britain running.

bank.q: Everyone who crosses the Channel illegally should be detained and deported, with no right to stay.
bank.ctx: This is a hardline stance on the small boats crossing the English Channel — tens of thousands a year: detain and deport everyone who arrives illegally, the thinking behind the (blocked) Rwanda deportation scheme. The stake is how Britain handles irregular Channel arrivals.

bank.q: Desperate people fleeing war are not criminals, and treating asylum seekers as an invasion shames Britain.
bank.ctx: This opposes that approach, arguing that people fleeing war and persecution are not criminals and that treating asylum seekers as an 'invasion' betrays British values and legal duties. The stake is compassion and law versus deterrence at the border.

bank.q: Brexit was a mistake and Britain should move back towards rejoining the EU.
bank.ctx: Brexit was Britain's 2020 departure from the European Union after the narrow 2016 referendum. This calls it a mistake — citing trade friction and economic drag — and wants Britain to move back toward the EU. The stake is whether to reverse the biggest political decision in a generation.

bank.q: Brexit restored British self-government and we should never surrender it back to Brussels.
bank.ctx: This defends Brexit as having restored British control over its own laws, borders, and money ('take back control'), and opposes surrendering that to Brussels again. The stake is national sovereignty versus the benefits of EU membership.

bank.q: The very richest should pay much more; Britain should tax wealth, not just income.
bank.ctx: This supports taxing the very richest much more, including a tax on accumulated wealth, not just income, to fund public services and reduce inequality. The stake is whether Britain should tax fortunes as well as earnings.

bank.q: Punishing wealth-creators with ever higher taxes just drives them, and their money, out of Britain.
bank.ctx: This argues that ever-higher taxes drive wealthy people, entrepreneurs, and their money out of Britain — pointing to 'non-doms' and millionaires leaving — which ultimately shrinks tax revenue. The stake is whether taxing wealth raises money or repels it.

bank.q: The benefits bill is out of control and should be capped hard to make work always pay.
bank.ctx: This argues Britain's welfare bill — swollen by rising disability and sickness claims — is out of control and should be capped so that work always pays more than benefits. The stake is controlling welfare spending and work incentives.

bank.q: Britain’s safety net has been cut to the bone; sanctions and caps just push disabled people and children into destitution.
bank.ctx: This argues Britain's safety net has already been cut to the bone by a decade of austerity, and that caps and sanctions push disabled people and children into destitution, driving the rise of food banks. The stake is whether welfare is too generous or too harsh.

bank.q: Britain must hit net zero even if it means higher costs and disruption now.
bank.ctx: 'Net zero' is Britain's legal target to cut greenhouse gases to net nil by 2050. This backs hitting it even at short-term cost, as a climate leader. The stake is how much economic pain is worth accepting now to meet the target.

bank.q: Net zero is an unaffordable middle-class vanity project that is wrecking British industry and household budgets.
bank.ctx: This argues net zero is an unaffordable project pushed by a comfortable middle class that is raising energy bills and hurting industry, while Britain's emissions are tiny globally. It fuelled backlash over boiler and car rules. The stake is whether the transition is being done too fast.

bank.q: Rail, water, and energy should be taken back into public ownership.
bank.ctx: This supports 'nationalisation' — bringing privatised rail, water, and energy back into public ownership — after years of complaints about fares, sewage spills, and bills. It was Labour policy under Corbyn. The stake is who should own Britain's essential services.

bank.q: State-run industries meant strikes, waste, and decline; private companies, properly regulated, run them better.
bank.ctx: This defends private ownership of those industries, arguing the nationalised versions before the 1980s meant strikes, underinvestment, and decline, and that regulation, not state control, is the answer. The stake is whether public or private hands run utilities better.

bank.q: Britain must build far more homes, even on protected green belt land, to fix the housing crisis.
bank.ctx: The 'green belt' is protected countryside ringing cities to stop urban sprawl. This supports building many more homes even there, to tackle a housing crisis of high prices and scarce supply. The stake is countryside protection versus desperately needed housing.

bank.q: Concreting over the countryside is not the answer; the green belt must be protected from developers.
bank.ctx: This defends the green belt and countryside from developers, arguing Britain should build on brownfield (previously used) land instead of concreting over nature. The stake is where new housing should go.

bank.q: Sentences are too soft; violent and repeat criminals should spend far longer behind bars.
bank.ctx: This argues sentences are too lenient and that violent and repeat offenders should serve much longer, reflecting 'tough on crime' politics. Prisons are already near capacity. The stake is whether harsher punishment makes the public safer.

bank.q: Locking more people up for longer has never cut crime; prevention and rehabilitation do.
bank.ctx: This argues that locking more people up for longer has not cut crime, that prisons are overcrowded 'universities of crime', and that prevention and rehabilitation work better — as lower-reoffending systems abroad suggest. The stake is what actually reduces offending.

bank.q: The authorities covered up the ethnicity of grooming gangs for years out of political correctness, and it must be said openly.
bank.ctx: This refers to organised sexual abuse by 'grooming gangs' in towns like Rotherham, and claims authorities hid the offenders' largely Pakistani-heritage background out of fear of appearing racist. Official inquiries confirmed failures to act. The stake is confronting a sensitive truth versus stoking prejudice.

bank.q: Framing child abuse as a problem of one ethnic group is a racist distortion of a crime found in every community.
bank.ctx: This argues that framing child sexual abuse as one ethnic group's problem is a racist distortion, since abuse occurs across all communities and most offenders nationally are white. The stake is how to discuss ethnicity and crime without scapegoating.

bank.q: People should be able to change their legal gender by self-declaration, without medical gatekeeping.
bank.ctx: This supports letting people change their legal gender by self-declaration, without a medical diagnosis — the reform Scotland passed but the UK government blocked. The stake is whether legal gender should rest on self-identification.

bank.q: A man cannot become a woman by filling in a form; the law must be based on biological sex.
bank.ctx: This is the gender-critical view, prominent in Britain's fierce debate: that a man cannot become a woman by filling in a form and that the law must rest on biological sex, for example in women's prisons, wards, and sport. The stake is how the law defines sex and gender.

bank.q: Scotland should become an independent country.
bank.ctx: This supports Scottish independence — Scotland leaving the United Kingdom, as the SNP campaigns for and as the 2014 referendum (55% No) rejected. Brexit, which Scotland opposed, revived the question. The stake is the break-up of the UK.

bank.q: Scotland is stronger inside the United Kingdom, and the independence question was settled in 2014.
bank.ctx: This opposes independence, arguing Scotland is stronger inside the UK's larger economy and shared institutions, and that the 2014 vote settled the matter 'for a generation'. The stake is keeping the United Kingdom together.

bank.q: The monarchy should be abolished and replaced with an elected head of state.
bank.ctx: This supports abolishing the monarchy and replacing the King with an elected head of state — a republic. Supporters object to inherited power and its cost. The stake is whether Britain should keep a hereditary head of state.

bank.q: The monarchy gives Britain stability and continuity that no politician could provide, and should be kept.
bank.ctx: This defends the monarchy as a source of stability, continuity, and national unity that stands above party politics, as it has for centuries. The stake is the value of a symbolic, non-political crown.

bank.q: Charging VAT on private school fees is fair: elite schooling should not get a tax break.
bank.ctx: This backs the government charging 20% VAT on private school fees, arguing elite education should not enjoy a tax break while state schools are stretched. About 7% of UK pupils attend private schools. The stake is fairness between private and state education.

bank.q: Taxing parents who sacrifice to educate their children just punishes aspiration and floods state schools.
bank.ctx: This opposes the private-school tax, arguing it punishes parents who sacrifice to educate their children, could force some pupils into an already-strained state system, and hits middle-income families, not just the rich. The stake is whether the policy is fair or spiteful.

bank.q: Multiculturalism has failed and produced divided communities that share nothing in common.
bank.ctx: This argues Britain's multiculturalism has failed, producing communities that live separate, parallel lives with little in common — a claim heard after riots and over integration. The stake is whether diversity without a shared culture divides Britain.

bank.q: Britain’s diversity is one of its greatest strengths, and multicultural cities are proof it works.
bank.ctx: This celebrates Britain's diversity as one of its greatest strengths, pointing to vibrant, successful multicultural cities like London. The stake is whether Britain's mix of cultures is a success or a problem.

bank.q: Islam is not compatible with British values.
bank.ctx: This argues Islam clashes with British values on free speech and equality — a view aired in debates over extremism and integration. Critics call it prejudice against millions of ordinary British Muslims. The stake is whether the concern is legitimate or bigoted.

bank.q: British Muslims are as much a part of this country as anyone, and their faith deserves equal respect.
bank.ctx: This holds that British Muslims are as much a part of the country as anyone and their faith deserves equal respect and protection. The stake is religious equality versus singling out one faith.

bank.q: Some races are simply more intelligent or capable than others.
bank.ctx: This is a statement of racial supremacism — the belief that some races are innately more intelligent or capable than others. It was the ideological engine of Nazism and the Holocaust, and of systems like slavery and apartheid. Modern genetics finds more variation within any racial group than between them, and the idea has no scientific standing.

bank.q: There is no hierarchy of races; the idea is pseudo-science with a shameful history.
bank.ctx: This states the principle of fundamental human equality: that no race is innately superior in intelligence or ability, and that racial hierarchies are discredited pseudo-science with a shameful history behind slavery and apartheid. It is the moral baseline of modern anti-discrimination law.

bank.q: People are being arrested for offensive posts and jokes; free speech in Britain is under real threat.
bank.ctx: This argues free speech in Britain is genuinely threatened, pointing to people being arrested or investigated over offensive social-media posts and jokes under communications and public-order laws. The stake is whether Britain polices speech too heavily.

bank.q: So-called free-speech warriors just want a licence to abuse minorities; hate speech laws protect people.
bank.ctx: This argues the free-speech complaint is often cover for wanting to abuse minorities without consequence, and that hate-speech laws protect vulnerable people from real harm. The stake is the line between free expression and hate.

bank.q: Police waste time policing tweets and pronouns while real crime goes uninvestigated.
bank.ctx: This argues police waste time on 'non-crime hate incidents' and policing online speech while burglaries and thefts go uninvestigated, reflecting frustration over charge rates. The stake is whether police priorities are misplaced.

bank.q: Online abuse and hate crime are real harms, and the police are right to take them seriously.
bank.ctx: This argues online abuse and hate crime cause real harm and that police are right to take them seriously, not just 'traditional' crime. The stake is whether such policing is a distraction or a duty.

bank.q: Britain should cut the foreign aid budget and spend the money at home.
bank.ctx: Britain commits 0.7% (recently cut to 0.5%) of national income to foreign aid. This wants that budget cut and spent at home instead. The stake is whether aid to poorer countries is a worthy commitment or a luxury.

bank.q: Foreign aid saves lives and buys Britain influence; slashing it is both cruel and short-sighted.
bank.ctx: This defends foreign aid as saving lives, fighting disease and poverty, and buying Britain 'soft power' and influence abroad, calling cuts both cruel and short-sighted. The stake is Britain's role and generosity in the world.

bank.q: Britain should sharply increase defence spending and keep arming Ukraine.
bank.ctx: This supports sharply higher defence spending and continued arming of Ukraine against Russia, as threats from Russia grow. The stake is how much Britain should invest in the military and Ukraine's defence.

bank.q: Pouring billions into weapons and foreign wars is money that should be fixing Britain at home.
bank.ctx: This argues the billions spent on weapons and foreign wars would be better used fixing Britain's own public services and cost-of-living problems. The stake is priorities between defence abroad and needs at home.

bank.q: Drug use should be treated as a health issue, and possession for personal use decriminalised.
bank.ctx: This supports treating drug use as a health issue and decriminalising possession for personal use, following evidence from countries like Portugal that this cuts deaths and crime. The stake is whether prohibition or a health approach works better.

bank.q: Going soft on drugs floods our streets with addiction and hands the profits to the gangs.
bank.ctx: This opposes softening drug laws, arguing it floods streets with addiction and hands profits to the criminal gangs behind 'county lines' dealing. The stake is whether easing drug laws helps users or empowers dealers.

bank.q: Access to abortion is a settled right and should if anything be made easier.
bank.ctx: This treats abortion — legal in Britain up to 24 weeks — as a settled right and would if anything ease access, for example by decriminalising it fully. The stake is protecting or expanding abortion rights.

bank.q: Abortion ends a human life and the time limits should be tightened, not loosened.
bank.ctx: This argues abortion ends a human life and that the 24-week time limit, high by European standards, should be tightened rather than loosened. The stake is the moral status of the unborn and the legal limit.

bank.q: Britain should scrap first-past-the-post and elect MPs by proportional representation.
bank.ctx: 'First-past-the-post' means whoever gets the most votes in each seat wins, which can produce big majorities on a minority of the national vote. This wants it replaced with proportional representation, matching seats to overall votes. The stake is how fairly votes translate into power.

bank.q: First-past-the-post gives Britain strong, stable governments, and we should keep it.
bank.ctx: This defends first-past-the-post, arguing it delivers strong, stable single-party governments and a clear local MP, whereas proportional systems bring unstable coalitions. The stake is stability versus proportionality in Britain's democracy.

bank.q: Workers need stronger unions and more rights, and the right to strike should be protected.
bank.ctx: This supports stronger trade unions and worker rights, and protecting the right to strike, after a wave of strikes over pay by nurses, rail and other workers. The stake is the balance of power between workers and employers.

bank.q: Union barons hold the country to ransom; strike laws should be tightened, not loosened.
bank.ctx: This argues powerful union leaders hold the country to ransom with strikes that disrupt millions, and that strike laws should be tightened, echoing the Thatcher-era reforms. The stake is curbing union power versus protecting workers' leverage.

bank.q: Terminally ill adults should have the legal right to an assisted death.
bank.ctx: This supports giving terminally ill adults the legal right to an assisted death — the subject of a live parliamentary vote — as legal in parts of Europe, Canada, and Australia. The stake is control over one's own death.

bank.q: Legalising assisted dying puts pressure on the vulnerable to die and crosses a line society should not cross.
bank.ctx: This opposes legalising assisted dying, warning it would pressure the vulnerable, elderly, or disabled toward death and change the doctor's role, pointing to concerns over how Canada's system has expanded. The stake is whether the safeguards can hold.

bank.q: The minimum wage should rise significantly, even if some businesses say they can’t afford it.
bank.ctx: This supports raising the minimum wage significantly, even against business objections, so that work pays a decent living. Britain's minimum wage is already among the higher ones internationally. The stake is a decent wage floor versus employer costs.

bank.q: Forcing wages up faster than productivity just closes small businesses and destroys entry-level jobs.
bank.ctx: This argues pushing wages up faster than productivity forces small businesses to cut jobs or close and fuels inflation. The stake is whether higher minimums help workers or cost them jobs.

bank.q: Children should be taught to take pride in Britain’s history, not to be ashamed of the Empire.
bank.ctx: This favours teaching children pride in Britain's history, including the Empire, rather than shame — a stance in the 'culture war' over statues and how history is taught. The stake is what story Britain tells about its imperial past.

bank.q: A country that hides the crimes of its Empire from schoolchildren is lying to them.
bank.ctx: This supports teaching the crimes of the British Empire — famines, slavery, colonial violence — honestly, arguing that glossing over them misleads schoolchildren. The stake is honesty versus pride in teaching the imperial past.

bank.q: Free trade and open global markets have made Britain richer and should be embraced.
bank.ctx: This defends free trade and open global markets as having made Britain, historically a trading nation, richer through cheaper goods and exports. The stake is the value of economic openness.

bank.q: Globalisation gutted Britain’s industrial towns and sold working communities out to cheap foreign labour.
bank.ctx: This argues globalisation gutted Britain's industrial towns — the closed mines, mills, and factories of the north and midlands — by sending jobs to cheaper labour abroad, feeding the resentment behind Brexit. The stake is who globalisation left behind.

bank.q: Protecting nature and wildlife should take priority over new roads, runways, and development.
bank.ctx: This puts protecting nature and wildlife ahead of new roads, airport runways, and housing, reflecting environmental opposition to projects like airport expansion. The stake is conservation versus development and growth.

bank.q: Endless environmental objections are strangling the growth and infrastructure Britain badly needs.
bank.ctx: This argues endless environmental objections and planning rules are strangling the growth, housing, and infrastructure Britain badly needs. The stake is whether green rules protect nature or block progress.

bank.q: Diversity and inclusion schemes in workplaces have gone too far and should be scrapped.
bank.ctx: This argues workplace diversity and inclusion schemes have gone too far into box-ticking and ideology and should be scrapped, echoing a wider backlash against 'woke' corporate policy. The stake is whether such schemes fix bias or impose it.

bank.q: Diversity schemes exist because discrimination is real, and scrapping them just protects the old boys’ club.
bank.ctx: This defends diversity schemes as a response to real discrimination, arguing scrapping them just protects the old, closed networks (the 'old boys' club') that kept women and minorities out. The stake is whether inclusion efforts are fair or unfair.

bank.q: Energy giants making record profits should face a much bigger windfall tax.
bank.ctx: A 'windfall tax' is a one-off levy on unusually large profits. This wants a bigger one on energy companies that made record profits during the price crisis, to fund help with bills. The stake is taxing extraordinary profits to ease the cost of living.

bank.q: Windfall taxes scare off the investment Britain needs to keep the lights on.
bank.ctx: This argues windfall taxes scare off the investment Britain needs in energy — including new North Sea and green projects — to keep the lights on. The stake is whether taxing profits raises useful money or deters investment.

bank.q: Long-standing traditions and institutions carry hard-won wisdom and should not be swept away for novelty.
bank.ctx: This is the conservative philosophy of tradition, associated with Edmund Burke: that long-standing customs and institutions hold the accumulated, hard-won wisdom of generations, so change should be gradual and cautious rather than sweeping away what works for untested ideas.

bank.q: Clinging to tradition for its own sake just lets the dead hand of the past block necessary change.
bank.ctx: This is the progressive reply, in the spirit of Thomas Paine's line that 'the dead should not govern the living': that treating tradition as sacred just lets the prejudices of the past block overdue reform — as appeals to tradition once defended slavery and denying women the vote.

bank.q: A good society depends far more on personal responsibility than on government support.
bank.ctx: This reflects a core right-leaning value: that a healthy society depends mainly on individuals taking responsibility for their own choices and lives, and that leaning too heavily on government breeds dependence and saps initiative.

bank.q: Blaming individuals for problems caused by an unequal system is how the comfortable excuse the suffering of others.
bank.ctx: This reflects a core left-leaning value: that many hardships — poverty, poor health, joblessness — stem from unfair systems and circumstances beyond personal control, so blaming individuals lets the comfortable ignore problems they benefit from or could help fix.

heroSub: 70 statements on the issues defining Britain right now: the NHS, immigration, Brexit, tax, crime, and net zero. Every position is asked twice with opposite framing, revealing both your party alignment and your framing bias.

context:
Politics in the United Kingdom: the landscape behind this test

The UK is a parliamentary democracy in which the government is drawn from the House of Commons and survives only while it holds a majority there. Commons elections use first-past-the-post, which tends to manufacture single-party majorities from vote shares well below fifty per cent and to punish parties whose support is spread evenly across the country.

A two-party system under strain

Labour and the Conservatives have alternated in government for a century, but the space around them has become crowded. The Liberal Democrats occupy a centrist, strongly pro-European position. Reform UK competes for the populist right. The Greens pull left on economics and environment. The Scottish National Party dominates a nation of the union outright, which no other party does.

Because of first-past-the-post, this fragmentation produces volatile and sometimes counter-intuitive results. A party can gain millions of votes and win almost no seats, while a modest national swing can produce a landslide in seats.

The cleavages that actually divide voters

Brexit reorganised British politics more thoroughly than any recent event. It cut across the old class alignment, pulling socially conservative working-class voters in post-industrial areas toward the Conservatives and university-educated professionals toward Labour and the Liberal Democrats. Those coalitions remain unstable.

Constitutional questions are unusually prominent. Scottish independence, the status of Northern Ireland, and the powers of the devolved administrations are live arguments about the shape of the state, not just about policy. Housing costs, the NHS, and immigration consistently rank among the issues voters name as most important.

How this maps onto the compass

The British economic centre sits to the left of the American one and to the right of the Nordic one. Public healthcare free at the point of use is settled consensus; the argument is over funding and delivery rather than principle. On governance, the UK combines a strong civil liberties tradition with a centralised state and few formal constitutional limits.

This test uses live British policy arguments rather than abstract statements. For the full profiles, see the UK party guides.
